text.p: The United States grabbed a
commanding five-point lead over the International team after
the opening day at the Presidents Cup Friday.
The Americans, more at home on the undulating greens,
played outstanding golf in front of their President, Bill
Clinton, to lead 7-1/2-2-1/2 at the Robert Trent Jones Golf
Club.
They won four of five morning fourball (better ball)
matches, and did not let up in the afternoon (alternate shot)
foursomes as they won three more matches, and halved another
to leave the Internationals in a deep hole.
In the inaugural Presidents Cup here two years ago, the US
was never headed after bolting to the same five-point lead
after the first day.
It was a similar story on Friday, as Fred Couples and
Davis Love led the U.S. onslaught by winning both their
matches against Greg Norman and Robert Allenby.
Love and Couples, winners of the past four World Cups, won
2 and 1 in the fourballs, then triumphed 1 up in the foursomes
when Norman and Allenby lost the final hole. Norman left his
60-foot putt five feet short, from where Allenby missed his
par-saving attempt to halve the hole.
Another American pairing, Mark O'Meara and David Duval,
also won both matches.
International team captain Peter Thomson paid credit to
Couples and Love: "They played superbly. I don't know anybody
who could have beaten them today," Thomson said.
"We're in trouble. I acknowledge that, and my team does
too. Our fellows aren't putting well. It's really only on the
greens where the matches have been lost. They're having
problems picking where to putt, and how hard to hit them.
These are very difficult greens."
The only Internationals to have a better than average day
were South African Ernie Els and Zimbabwean Mark McNulty. They
beat Scott Hoch and Mark Brooks 2 up in the fourballs, then
halved their foursomes contest with Corey Pavin and Phil
Mickelson.
The star-studded International team looks at least as
strong as the American side on paper, but reputations could
for little in the heat of matchplay.
Norman, the world's top-ranked player, acknowledged as
much when he said of his afternoon loss: "We three-putted
three times. You don't do that out here and expect to win."
American captain Arnold Palmer did not believe his players
would be overconfident going into the second day: "I think
they're smarter than that," he said.
